utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, a few matters. There was a confusion about a video yesterday, Mr. Groome, which was supposed to have been provided but the wrong one was provided. Or Mr. Traldi. What is it? Was it P287?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, P287. And my understanding is we've provided it -- a CD to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that now has been done. There is one other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since it is now there, I think yesterday it was MFI'd and therefore P287 is now admitted into evidence. The -- I'd like to briefly deal with Witness RM081. On the 27th of September the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the Chamber augment the protective measures currently in place for Witness RM081 and order that his testimony in the present case be received with voice distortion. On the 28th of September, 2012, the witness informed the Chamber in court that it did not oppose the augmentation of the protective measures. The Chamber notes that in the Krajisnik and Karadzic trials, Witness RM081 testified under pseudonym and with image distortion. Pursuant to Rule 75(F) of the Rules, the protective measures ordered in the first proceedings remain in force in the present proceedings. As no Chamber remains seized of the first proceedings and the Chamber is currently seized of the second proceedings within the meaning of Rule 75(G) of the Rules, it finds that it has jurisdiction to rule on the motion. In addition, considering that the only Judge from the first proceedings who remains a Judge is the Presiding Judge in the present case, the Chamber finds that the requirement of Rule 75(I) of the Rules is satisfied. Further, in light of the declaration of the Prosecution's investigator confirming the witness's consent to the requested augmentation, the Chamber is of the view that the requirement of Rule 75(J) of the Rules is also satisfied. Having regard to the Prosecution's submissions that Witness RM081 feared to be recognised and noting that the Defence does not object the augmentation of the protective measures, the Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution's motion and orders that Witness RM081's testimony be received with -- apart from the already -- apart from the protective measures already in place to be received also with voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well I misspoke that the witness informed the Chamber, it was the Defence that informed the Chamber that it did not oppose the augment ation of the protective measures. Could the witness - not that witness, but could the present witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While he is being brought in two quick matters. First as you suggested yesterday, I'd seek leave to replace Exhibit P290, which is the one with a small set of handwritten numbers towards the top, with a clean unmarked version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And second, I misspoke yesterday at transcript page 3461, line 9, it appears where I referred to paragraph 4 in Exhibit P283, it should be 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A few lines further down you refer to paragraph 24 so that is clear. And the page references which was page 5 was okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I said that the replacement of P290, that leave was granted, I'd forgotten that I should instruct the Registry to replace the translation, the English version, by the new version that has been provided by the Prosecution. That is, without handwritten numbers on it. Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. May I again invite you all not to speak at the same time and to make a pause between question and but also between answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm fine. Can we concentrate and go through the questions quickly.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I will do my best to give you as short answers as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked you about the new reorganisation [as interpreted] that was requested by the SDS and after that we moved on and concluded that the SDS had left or walked out of the parliament --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right, you're interpreted Mr. Lukic as saying "the new reorganisation." Was it the reorganisation or was it regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] New regionalisation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll just correct it on the script, regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were a deputy in the parliament. The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it possible for it to be used on its own or was it obligatory for that to be used within the constitution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina pertained to Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, part of the constitution that regulated relations with Yugoslavia were referred to the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you aware that each of the three constituent nations - Muslims, Croats, and Serbs - had right to veto some decisions in order to protect their national interests?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were granted the right to veto but only within the jurisdictions where this veto can be applied. It did not apply to any decisions whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was one of those rights the right to use veto if somebody tried to secede the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was a major constitutional issue and unfortunately I'm not able to discuss these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court Mr. Sejmenovic's statement, P283. P283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page and paragraph Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, in this paragraph, you say that the SDS pursued and implemented the same policy in Prijedor. It sought to divide Prijedor into two municipalities with institutions divided along ethnic lines. In other municipalities, at the same time, the SDS separated their own municipalities. For example, the municipality of Kljuc. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Separated from what? I am not aware of the municipality of Kljuc being separated from any -- anything. I'm not aware of any municipality being separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the fact that SDA had power in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know - it does not necessarily mean that it's true - that SDA established the municipality of Kljuc parallel to the municipality of Kljuc where the SDS was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct. There may have been some attempts to do that, but I don't think that any legislature underpinned such a development and that would be the only proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No separation was conducted at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And any separation was actually illegal from the point of view of the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at the time not only did Yugoslavia break up but the same happened with Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was not disintegrating. As far as I know the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina was fully functional, whereas the Yugoslav parliament did not exist anymore. Also functioning was the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, on the other hand, Yugoslavia had no longer the Presidency that it had had earlier. However, it was functioning with difficulties but there were -- because there were some political structures that were obstructing the whole process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Assembly and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina were functioning without Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Without only one part of representatives of the Serbian people. Serb representatives were still present in the parliament but they were not from the SDS, but, rather, from some other parties. In all fairness I have to say that the majority of deputies were members of the SDS, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many Serb representatives were in the parliament that were voted by the people to become members, or were people simply installed into the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We shall never find out who voted for whom because the ballot was a secret one. All we know is the fact that in the parliament there were certain percentages of deputies from all parties and from all nationalities. This is the only thing that we know exactly. There were manipulations and speculations about who voted for whom, but as I said since this procedure is free and secret we would never know. I repeat, there were still Serb representatives in the parliament but to a lesser percentage because the majority of deputies were from the SDS and they left the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we are going to discuss this issue with some other witnesses as well. That's it for now. Now, let's look at paragraph 10. You say that: "The SDS rejected attempts at interethnic co-operation and SDA proposals for the formation of interethnic patrols." At the time, were actually any joint police and army patrols set up?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 relates to the events in Prijedor municipality. It's not specifically said in this paragraph but it was said in the talks that we previously had, and we dealt with some very specific situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now paragraph 11. You say that: "The Prijedor SDS created a shadow government with parallel bodies." That happened in February 1992 when Prijedor SDS demanded the dissolution of the existing municipal assembly and the calling of an early election. SDS was in power, together with SDA, in Prijedor at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the party who is in power is seeking new elections.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And they provided a specific reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reasons that I managed to find out in the minutes of the assembly meeting chaired by Mr. Cehajic was, in fact, to obstruct the functioning of the municipality, and he insisted that the chief of police be appointed from among the Serbs. Are you aware of any other reasons that they had cited?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The SDS construed this in their own way, this proposal. Basically this proposal was prompted by their wish to have specific positions in the municipality filled by the SDS regardless of the agreed division of power and the solutions offered in that sense, whether they do it themselves or whether the SDA do it, and to offer the other side to take half of it, but that was eventually found to be unacceptable by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in the course of talks and negotiations at the republic of -- at the level of the republic, it was agreed that chief of police would be someone from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know there was no such agreement, particularly not at the level of the republic. They may have put forward such a request but there was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the chief proposed by the SDS, that this proposal was rejected in Sarajevo. Two appointments were rejected which prolonged the whole procedure whilst there were no real reasons for the rejections?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The SDA and the SDS had a very firm agreement concerning the division of posts. The SDA honoured this agreement to the very end which cannot be said about the SDS because they wanted to have the police and the public auditing service. Finally they agreed to a 50-50 decision but they continued to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to hear what the other side will have to sigh about this, but that's going to happen in the future. Now let's talk about the events preceding the takeover of power on -- in Prijedor, and we shall start with paragraph 13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you referring to future evidence to be presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No one here is supposed to present evidence on one side or another side. We only hear evidence, witnesses who will testify about the truth and not about being member of one side or a member of any other side. Just for you to know. Apart from that, it was not necessary to announce to this witness what evidence you will present, perhaps challenging what this witness said. That's irrelevant for the witness to know and the Chamber will find out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Only one clarification: I didn't mean the other side of the proceeding but the other side of those negotiations. I though the members of SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My -- as a matter of fact, the other side. Yes. If the other side of the negotiations tells us the truth, then for both sides we hear the same evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say after Croatia demanded independence the Serb population in Croatia mutinied at the support of authorities in Belgrade, and these regions were, after that, under the control of Serbs, and the army was under the control of Serbs. Could we also agree that issue, too, is a legal one and that you did not do any research into it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I did not do any research. I know about it as much as I followed events and listened to the media and various political positions expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraph 14, please. You say: "Serb authorities in Serbia began broadcasting propaganda in Bosnia-Herzegovina and blocking the broadcast of non-Serb programmes. Some TV repeaters were taken control of." Which non-Serb programmes were blocked by the authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We in Bosnia-Herzegovina were used to watching the TV programme broadcast by the TV Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, we were able also to watch programmes from other republics. There was a TV study called Jutel which was an anti-war one, and their programme was intensively broadcast on BHTV. Then the army, with the support of the police as far as I know, took over and seized the main TV transmitter in Bosnia-Herzegovina, called Lisina, and from that moment on in Bosnian Krajina you could not watch BHTV anymore and solely TV Serbia was broadcast. And sometime later also the local Serbian TV. And there you could see programmes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say the Serb authorities in Serbia began broadcasting propaganda and blocking the broadcast of non-Serb problems. How were the Serb authorities in Serbia able to block anything in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This statement summarizes all the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean you could describe it in detail?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I can tell you anything. You just have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serb authorities in Serbia block the repeater in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There are military authorities, police authorities, and civil -- civilian authorities. It's not the president of the parliament in Serbia who came to block this repeater but a general did, and somebody must have made the political decision to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: At that time, did TV Sarajevo stop taking over programmes from TV Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when this TV repeater was blocked, or just before that, we were able to watch on TV both Bosnian and Croatian programmes and programmes from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It's the beginning of the second half or towards the end of 1991. I'm not really good at dates, and it's -- it was too long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from whether the level of detail of some of the matters which are discussed assist the Chamber, one of the last questions was: When that TV repeater was blocked, or just before -- no. That -- you were asked: "At that time, did TV Sarajevo stop taking over programmes from TV Belgrade?" If you know, tell us; if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I did not see any particular change in the programming of TV Sarajevo before that. And I don't remember that it stopped taking over Belgrade programmes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you put a question, it's always good to get an answer to that question as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, are you aware that armed units of the Territorial Defence of Kljuc which were fighting against Serb forces blew up the TV repeater in Ramici village?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that and I don't know to what time-period you are referring to. It was certainly not the same time-period we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not aware of that. That's an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any time? At any time. Did you hear about it in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not even hear of its existence because it was insignificant. The main repeater was at Lisina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not hear about it. That is an answer to the question. How important it was or may have been or whether you should have known about its existence, that's not the question. Please limit your answers to what you are asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the SDA insisted that only SDA people be employed at TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even if there is documentation to support it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there is documentation, but I spent a lot of time there and I don't think that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see that a security detail of the SDA was guarding TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You go on to say that the JNA began arming the Serb population in Prijedor. And you say it was unlawful. Can we agree that the war was going on in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there was a general mobilisation declared in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I believe this arming took place even before the mobilisation. But, all right. Let's take it that it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that anyone who responded to the mobilisation call-up received a weapon, regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The army knows best what it did with those who responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In fact you don't know whom the army was arming?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph you're reading, it's about three particular situations, and the arming was taking place outside of any military rules or regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you study the military regulations on the arming of the population?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service. I know -- Your Honours, I have to say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at the same time. You were asked whether you studied the military regulations on the arming of the population. Did you; or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not study them. But I do have experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the former Yugoslavia, at the time you are talking about, there was a system of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the system of All People's Defence, and I read a course for two years in school named All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the front line in Croatia held by the 55th Corps was over 800 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the periphery stretches in Bosnia-Herzegovina were armed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know what happened in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that you served in the artillery?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your weapon?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: A 105-millimetre Howitzer in an artillery garrison that had weapons of 105 to 155 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend drills using live ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Krivolak?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: To the Bulgarian border once and some place called Pasuljarske Livade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get a rank after serving the army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps private first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do that Howitzer 105-millimetres?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I was the gunner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something about the takeover in Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Mladic made a gesture again. Last warning. There's no need to comment, even by gestures, on any answer of the witness, what he did in the army, yes or no. Mr. Mladic, this is the last warning. Once again and you're out of court. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the takeover in Prijedor, you say all Muslims were dismissed from their work. But I would like to focus with you on the period from the takeover of power until the 22nd May 1992. Would you agree that after the takeover only politicians lost their jobs in Prijedor; in other words, people who held high posts as members of a certain party because the SDS had taken over power?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the first few days it was only the politicians. Later, it was teachers, foremen in factories and other staff, then lower-ranking staff, and then everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the 22nd, those people who did not come to work for three days lost their jobs and that was completely legal, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot talk about individual cases and individual fates. There were people who came to work and were unable to get in. There were people who worked in banks and who were prevented from coming through the door. And if the -- their administration later treated it as a failure to report to work, that was only symptomatic of the whole situation and the interrelations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say in the same paragraph: "Later on, movement from non-Serb areas towards Prijedor was prohibited." Who made this prohibition?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We could see it only happening. We could see only the execution of that prohibition. Of course, we did not see the document itself. Military check-points were set up in Orlovci, and in the period we are discussing, you could not pass through that check-point anymore. You had to ask for a special permit, and my trip to Prijedor -- or rather, our trip to Prijedor was with a permit to go through that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So movement was controlled. It was not prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Most people were turned back. And people who wanted to go to town in order to go to work, and people who wanted to go to town for other reasons, to go shopping, were turned back. And on what grounds individuals were allowed to go through, I don't know. I know only it was up to the authorities and those who controlled those check-points. On the route to Banja Luka, on the other hand, it was impossible to go through at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it apply in the direction from Kozarac? Could you get through from Ljubija, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "Non-Serb teachers were removed from schools." When were teachers removed from schools?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Teachers were removed from schools shortly before the takeover. Only one person, one lady, remained working in the school, and she was married to a Serb. And it was from her that we were able to get some more information about the cases in her school. And it is certain that the same thing was going on in other schools. Some of our SDA activists were teachers in schools, and they told us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we make a break, Your Honour? Obviously Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take an early break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. Any checkups should be done within the next 20 minutes, to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to -- Mr. Mladic, thumbs up is a gesture which is unacceptable; by the way, the same would be true for thumbs down. Just for you to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sejmenovic, we were discussing the topic of teacher dismissals. Did you learn that the schools in Prijedor actually stopped working on the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly following the period we discussed, they continued working for about between seven to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And before the takeover, apparently you seemed to say that some were fired before the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I have never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought you just did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pause between question and answer, and between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is in the transcript. Line 8, page 18: [In English] "Teachers were removed from schools shortly before the takeover."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Attack on?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Before the military coup, before the attack on Kozarac and Hambarine. The dismissals took place after the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 - and we'll dwell on it a bit longer - you say that: "The non-Serb workers who tried to go to work were sent home. The police chief Hasan Talundzic had been delegated by the SDA and told us that non-Serb police officers were disarmed and sent home." Is it correct that the policemen in question refused to acknowledge the authority of the SDS after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The policemen were disarmed in the police station. Later on, some of them were offered a possibility -- later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, the question was a different one. The question was whether Mr. Talundzic refused to acknowledge the authority of the SDS after the takeover. Did he, or did he not, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talundzic refused and he could no longer retain his function -- or keep his function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 18. It reads -- well, there you discuss Exhibit 06908, which is P285.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You quoted part of that document. "Only persons who are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina can be placed in the management positions in enterprises." Did the situation allow that at such time people loyal to the other side should be allowed to stay in management positions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is -- this is a parastate document which was put in the place by paralegal authorities. It goes directly against the state law. We abided by the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its lower instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we come to the domain of law again, and we have already established that are you not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: To assert this, one need not be a lawyer. It is a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Facts are that you did not honour the laws of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We honoured the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Autonomous Region of Krajina was a para-state at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was the JNA the official armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Up to a certain point, but afterwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of May it still was, but it was duty-bound to act within Bosnia-Herzegovina in keeping with instructions of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It did not. It acted contrary to the will of the Supreme Commander who was part of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, the Supreme Commander of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the president of the BiH Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina the army was not independent. It could act in co-operation with the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you please allow the witness to -- where is he answering to your question, allow him to finish and not interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was this: In your view, was the president of Presidency in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Supreme Commander of the JNA, which is what you just said, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the JNA -- well, perhaps I formed it poorly. They had their commander, and in the territory of that republic, the army could not behave as if the republic did not exist. It could only act in co-ordination with the president of the republic. However, it acted as if there was no president or parliament. It also supported parastates in their process of creation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we go on with this for the next hour, it seems that we have a rather chaotic examination mainly dealing with legal issue where the witness firmly wants to support the idea that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, was not a authority which deserved to be obeyed, and where you, Mr. Lukic, seem to emphasise that the JNA was still the official army within the former Yugoslavia at that time. Where the witness wants to then introduce other elements of the way how -- what may have been the formal army of the former Yugoslavia, what limits there were in the way they would exercise the functions. This is a chaotic discussion. Most important - and I think that has become clear to the Chamber - is that there were huge disputes about state and armed forces and police authority. I take it that the Chamber is not assisted by all the details as we were not assisted by details on where exactly the witness served in the army, whether he was dealing with Howitzers or mortars, or whatever. At least not without a follow-up. The Chamber does not understand how it would serve it in making the determinations it will have to make. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I'm going through witness's statement. This is in his statement, and I have to question him on this. If he says he knows, let him explain. I think that he helped us every time when he tried to explain something. I cannot leave it this way without asking him. Otherwise it would -- because tomorrow it will be very easy to contradict his testimony. But if we don't have his testimony, it wouldn't be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you could not ask him questions about what he says, but it expands far beyond that and that is what the Chamber does not consider in the interests of the justice at this moment. Ask him questions about when teachers were fired or not. He explained that to us as what was the takeover, what he understands that. And the more we go into details and the more you start responding to all kind of minor elements of his answers, we get further and further away from what this case is really about. This is what is the Chamber's guidance at this moment for the further cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the SDS at the time, which is the 11th of May, asked for loyalty not only by Serbs -- by Muslims but by Serbs as well. We can see item 6 where it says that all able-bodied men who had fled the region of the Krajina should immediately return to their municipalities. The next paragraph in item 6: "All persons who fail to respond to the above calls shall be forbidden to return to their homes in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and all their movable and immovable property shall be confiscated." Does this pertain to Muslims, Croats or Serbs; or perhaps all of them?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Reading paragraph 6, it seems it applies to all. And the last sentence, in and of itself, speaks volumes about illegitimacy of this document and the person who put it in place. Confiscating property may not be the consequence of a failure to respond to a military call-up. It was not the case in any system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not. But if such law is in force, then it would be.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was no such law, and this is a testimony to what kind of creation it was. This sentence has no basis in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina or any other legal act that I am familiar with through my work in the parliament. The Autonomous Region was a parastate creation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that non-Serb were driven out of the factories. How many factories were there in Prijedor and how many of them were operational at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know any details about it, but there were several factories. The wood pulp factory was operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that it stopped its production because it could no longer receive raw materials from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know from others that one part of that factory called Fel Pak [phoen] still worked. There were some other facilities that were operational, such as those servicing the railway, transport companies, some other public companies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was not only the dismissal of employees but that there was a complete stop of all economic activity in Prijedor which was directly connected to the attack on Prijedor and the incidents in Kozarac and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I wasn't in the town of Prijedor itself. I don't think it could have brought about a complete stop to all economic activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say -- or, rather, you are critical of the Serbs boasting about taking over Prijedor without firing a single bullet. That's in paragraph 20. Is it a fact that the power was taken without firing a single bullet?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what you read was only half of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the rest in your statement. I'm just asking if it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let's move to paragraph 21. You say that the main personalities were on the Crisis Staff, and then you name Stakic, Kovacevic, and Drljaca, and you added "... as well as military commanders." Were military commanders members of the Prijedor Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Under the laws, the notion of Crisis Staff during the time of war was precisely defined, and it was prescribed who members were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether, according to these provisions, were military commanders members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: If there is a garrison in a municipality, each garrison commander becomes a member of the Crisis Staff by virtue of his position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is only now, Mr. Lukic, that the transcript of the answer was completed. I don't have to explain to you how could you do it. Just do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court 1D323.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic kindly be advised to wait for the interpretation to end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a decision regulating the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality from May 1992. There is a description of how it is going to be organised. And then, under Article 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is page 3 in e-court in B/C/S, and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Article 4 reads that: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality shall consist of a president, a vice-president, and nine members." And down there, these representatives who are to sit on the Crisis Staff are being listed. I can't see anywhere under this article any mention of a member of a military. At that time, were you aware of this document? And what is exactly your source of information? Can you tell us in which document you found that military personnel were members of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This document was adopted by new authorities in May of 1992, as you can see on the front page. The legislature that was in force prior to that prescribed who and under what conditions can become a member of municipal Crisis Staff and how the staff is formed and how it functions. So according to the former legitimate laws, the Crisis Staff looked differently, and it was obligatory for garrison commanders - in the municipalities where there were garrisons - to become members of a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge if at that time this decision was implemented in Prijedor municipality or if those laws that you just mentioned were implemented, although you never told us specifically which legal document you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the takeover of power, the legislature that had been in force before that were applicable, and a Crisis Staff met once with the Chief Cehajic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the military person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the military person you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vladimir Arsic, the garrison commander. But that was before the takeover of power. There was an initiative that: Due to the prevailing situation, a Crisis Staff should be set up and meet. According to the municipal statute, this initiative was implemented and they met, and Colonel Arsic was present in one of the meetings when discussions were conducted with the president of the municipality. But I underline, once again, that that was before the takeover of power. When the military coup was carried out, the Serbian authorities took power and we now see on our screens a new document, which is different from the one that stipulated the organisation of the Crisis Staff in the preceding period. Here, in this specific instance, you can see that the head for housing and utility affairs shall become a member of a Crisis Staff. This is nonsense because in the previous legislature this person could not be a member of a Crisis Staff on any grounds. I can tell you who was supposed to be member of Crisis Staff according to the old legislature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you present this as a decision. It, however, on its face -- it seems to be a draft. The date on which it apparently was adopted is not there. So, therefore, could you inform us on whether this was ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document, Your Honour, was used in Stakic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not an answer to my question. There may have been -- I'm not saying that any unwise things were done in the Stakic trial. I do not know, as a matter of fact. But what I'm asking now is where this document appears at face value to be without a date when it was adopted, without, in the original, the signature where you would expect it. And at the bottom again not any adoption date. I was just interested in the status of this document which you presented as a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's obvious from the records, from the sessions of the Crisis Staff, that were held after the -- the takeover.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Lukic kindly be advised to let the interpreters end the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat everything you said now. Because you have not allowed the interpreters to translate my words. So please re-start. I think you wanted to say that it's obvious from the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Records of the sessions of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality held that this act was in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would say, I will tender into evidence the proceedings of the Crisis Staff on that and that date when it was adopted, and I suggest it to be tendered from the bar table, that is an answer. But this is all rather vague, and the Chamber very much insists on facts rather than on debates. But I do understand that it's your position that it was adopted. We still do not when it was adopted. And we're looking forward to receiving further information on this document which, on its face, is a draft and nothing else. It may be that it was adopted without any changes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform Your Honours that this document is received from the Prosecution. It bears their number. And we'll have a witness on Crisis Staffs in this trial proposed by the Prosecution. So I think it's the best time to discuss this document and similar in length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. No problem with that. But, Mr. Lukic, that it was received from the Prosecution means that a document which, on its face, seems to be a draft, was received from the Prosecution. If you receive a draft, and if you present it as a decision, then you need to explain, and I now do understand that you are going to explain. Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Sejmenovic. Paragraph 22 of your statement. You speak about the period when the Army of Republika Srpska was established and the intensification of co-operation with the Crisis Staff. And you say under paragraph 22: "The JNA withdrew from B and H in mid-May 1992 but in reality did not withdraw. They just changed their name. The officers called themselves the Serb army, and the troop numbers increased even more in the area of Prijedor ..." My question is: You are testifying about Prijedor. Can you tell me, the soldiers who were originally from Serbia, did they leave Prijedor; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, only one small group of conscripts who were stationed in the area of Mrakovica and the barracks there, but in non-combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who remained, were they from Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro, or were they from Bosnia and Herzegovina and specifically the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The majority of them were locals. I'm talking about the mobilised reserve forces who became part of the establishment force of the 5th Kozara. The Command Staff remained, according to the decision they should have left. And, of course, the weapons remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this - and this is something that we already discussed with some military personnel from the command of the 5th Corps. Now, I'm going to ask you: After the 28th of June, when corridor was open and people were able to leave the territory of Bosnian Krajina, can you tell us exactly by name who remained in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 28th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On 28th of June, I was completely alone on the ground. I had no contact or communication with anyone. Slightly after that, I entered the Trnopolje camp and I obtained certain information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this information that you acquired, can you tell us now that you don't know who from the officers from Serbia and Montenegro remained in the RS, or don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know any particulars about military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You should make a pause between question and answer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 23 now. After the takeover of power in Prijedor by the SDS, did you attend any assembly meetings, the rump assembly that existed in Prijedor at the time, and did you attend any Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not after the takeover of power, but I did do so before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude that you don't know what were the relationships between the Crisis Staff and the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of power, yes, I know because we were present at the meeting where personnel from the army and Republika Srpska were as well as members of the Crisis Staff. They had enjoyed full co-operation amongst themselves. However, the army had last say on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarification. In the statement, you say that: "In the municipal assembly, Arsic and Zeljaja would use 'we' to describe themselves and the SDS politicians." If you did not attend any of the municipal assembly meetings, how did you know the exact use of language as you described in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in paragraph 23, it says at the beginning "After the VRS was created," but in actual fact this paragraph covers a longer period of time. Before the takeover of power, Arsic and Zeljaja attended a number of meetings of the municipal assembly where I myself was present too. And this word "we" was used to refer to all those who were backing the policy of joining the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where paragraph 23 suggests that things changed after the VRS was created, saying that the relationship became more direct, illustrated by the use of the word "we," that was a situation that existed already before. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is. And at the meeting that I attended, they used this word "we."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what you said before, and I pointed at the fact that this apparently was not a change after the moment you described in paragraph 23 but what was happened already before. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement dated 29 May, in paragraph 2 in B/C/S, the page is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Co-counsel please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And paragraph 4 is on 012480 -- 82, you say the following: "The orders to go into battle to go into attack could be issued exclusively by military commanders. Only they were able to give orders to fire weapons or artillery. However, the decision to go into battle at all was a political decision. In this case, either taken by the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council from Prijedor." You talk about the attack and Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber is not aware of this statement. Doesn't have access to it. Therefore, could you please show it to us because we want to know what the context is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just planned to ask this witness would he say the same today. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, if you refer -- then you can ask him without referring to that statement. You can ask this question and then be satisfied that it's the same or whether it's different and then put to him, if it is different, what he said at the time. But you're quoting from a statement, and the Chamber wants to have access to that statement in order to be better able to appreciate and to evaluate the evidence the witness gives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't -- we didn't upload this statement into the system, Your Honours, so I'm not able to do that. So I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that there was a political decision to attack Hambarine issued by the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council from Prijedor, a decision that the army executed in that attack?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you referred to, I said that on principle - and generally speaking - there has to be a political decision in order to use force, and the army gets orders along its chain of command and executes those orders. Now which political authority runs the army is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see in e-court 1D322. This is a report from the Ministry of Interior, Security Services Centre Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor. It's a report on reception centres in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the B/C/S - and that's the last paragraph on page 2 in B/C/S and also page 2, the second paragraph from the top - it says: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality has decided to carry out a military intervention in this village in order to disarm and capture known perpetrators of crimes against soldiers. The army has intervened and placed Hambarine village under control." Is that your experience from that time, from Prijedor, that the Crisis Staff ordered the army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: My experience is that the army in Prijedor received orders from the military command in Banja Luka; whereas, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality, in my opinion, could not issue orders to the Banja Luka Corps. There had to be a higher authority to order such action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Later on you spoke about Omarska, and since we have this document on the screen already, I'll ask you a few questions. On page 4 in B/C/S -- bear with me a moment. I can't find this paragraph in English for the time being. We'll move onto the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 8 in B/C/S, and page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the fifth paragraph from the top in B/C/S, and also fifth paragraph under chapter 3 in English of this report of the public security station in Prijedor, it says: "The investigating centre of POWs in Omarska and the transit facility Keraterm directly -- are directly secured by employees of the police in keeping with the decision of the Crisis Staff, considering that it has been assessed that in view of the numbers of the population, the area affected by armed conflict, the army does not have enough resources to take over these facilities too." In your statement, paragraphs 52 and on, you mentioned that you used to see army troops in Omarska in the camp itself. In several places you saw soldiers based, and they also walked around between hangars. You also saw people in army uniform. How could you determine inside Omarska, in the very centre where people were placed, who was a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Partly judging by the uniforms, and I also got some information from speaking to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from speaking to others, did you hear a name of any of these army members and to what unit that they belonged or the name of any unit?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Such personal information, I was unable to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that many people were convicted for Omarska, both before this Tribunal and before the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know there have been convictions, but I don't know how many. I did not follow that closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these judgements found that only policemen worked in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. And from my experience, there were not policemen alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But as you said, you have no specific examples to offer to counter these judgements of both the Tribunal and the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know first or last names or their war-time assignments, not concerning any individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. [In English] Is it convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we had a relatively late start, isn't it? So let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you say: "Slobodan Kuruzovic, an SDS official, was at the meeting, and he later became commander of the Trnopolje camp." Since you were active on the political scene at that time, do you know what position Slobodan Kuruzovic had in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the specific position but he was a prominent member. I believe he was on the Municipal Board, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also speak about the -- the ultimatum to turn over 5.000 or 7.000 weapons, and you say at that time in Kozarac there was no such number of weapons. Did you participate in the arming of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the shipments of weapons were brought to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There were no shipments of weapons to Kozarac. I have no such information. People did buy individually when they were able to. There's no question of organised arming because I would have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would you have known about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Because after the takeover our very existence was in jeopardy, and the issue of weapons was a vital issue. There were no weapons. People tried to make them by hand. If there had been weapons, there would have been no need to make them by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were an advocate of arming yourselves rather than surrendering weapons at the meetings you had in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's not true. What is true is that I advocated honouring the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, expanding the Territorial Defence, and letting it do its job because we had no guarantees that we could stop bloodshed by any other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "to expand the Territorial Defence," does it mean to increase the number of people and the number of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It means to organise the necessary defence in case non-Serb villages and populations are attacked. That means the most essential defence, only defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you're still not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I have answered the question. That has been discussed. We've dealt with it. The question was to accept an ultimatum we could not abide by. Your Honours, the situation was clear: Either return 7.000 rifles ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've told us that already. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you just say? What, in your understanding, was organising essential defence? Does it mean filling the Territorial Defence with people and replenishing it with weapons? You are giving me political boiler plates. I'm asking you were you advocating the purchase or acquisition of weapons and organising fighting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are talking about a -- the moment when we were under an ultimatum. There was more time to acquire weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you advocating the purchase of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that time one could not advocate anything anymore. We were under blockade and encircled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you could or not, the question is: Did you advocate the purchase of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we had been able to, I would have acquired planeloads, including tanks. But it was not possible anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were in favour of getting arms. Did you ever -- was it only your inner thoughts or did you ever express that view in the presence of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a life-and-death need, but it was no longer possible even in theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I really have to urge you that you answer the questions that are put to you. I didn't ask you whether it was a life-and-death need. I asked you whether you expressed those thoughts in the presence of others. That was my question. Did you; or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's an impossible question. The discussion was whether to return weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it is not an impossible question. I just asked you whether your inclination, your wish, to buy weapons, whether you kept that for yourself or whether you ever shared that with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had neither the wish nor the means any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have acquired planeloads of weapons but it was not possible anymore. This expresses clearly at one point in time that you wished --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you ever share that thought with others? You don't have to tell me that at a certain moment that you had given up on making it possible. Did you ever share that thought with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall -- well, could it be specified what point in time we're discussing? If we are discussing the meeting in Kozarac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- I said: Did you ever. That means all times you can specify when you did share it or, as I do understand, from what moment on you did not express that wish anymore. It's for you to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the ultimatum was issued, when any further talks were interrupted with Zeljaja. I was afraid at that point in time that if we surrendered even a minimum amount of weapons that what would follow would be a massacre. Then I expressed that I was afraid to have the weapons returned for the fear of us being finished if we did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that doesn't say anything about whether you shared the wish to buy weapons because that was the question -- the question was about that. But do I understand that after the ultimatum was made, that you at least wished to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never discussed any procurement of weapons. At no point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think it's time for a break. Witness, could I really urge you not to tell us what's on your mind but rather focus on what you're asked and to give answers to that. If I would ask you whether you arrived at a certain moment -- at a certain place by car, then you can start telling us about how many bicycles are available and whether you could have taken a tram or a plane. But the question simply is: Did you arrive by car. This is, of course, just an example. Think about it during the break. Try to focus your answers on the questions put to you, rather than to tell us about bicycles, planes, and trams. You may follow the usher. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at quarter past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, perhaps I raise a very short question. You gave us the conclusions which were sent to the president of the municipality personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under 3 I read: "We hereby express our support for the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Now this was apparently a conclusion reached by that same Crisis Staff, so I was a bit surprised and wondered whether there's any translation issue. Because it says we support ourselves. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have no further problems with that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sejmenovic, in paragraphs 29 to 31, you discuss the attempt to expand the TO in Kozarac. In paragraph 30, you say that the TO called on people to put themselves at its disposal. Did you have any problem with the -- with the response or was the response a good one?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I did not get involved directly as I was not neither competent nor had the authority to deal with it, but I do not recollect any problems with people responding. It was quite the other way around actually. This was put in place as a result of the pressure put on by the population itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, by the way, I had forgotten tell you we have considered how much time there would be for cross-examination. Having considered all the elements, which would include the certain level of irresponsiveness of the witness, we expect you to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I expect the same, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that over three and a half thousand people responded?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what number of people put themselves at their disposal, but there must be lists in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next chapter deals with the campaign of expulsion in Prijedor. In paragraph 33, you discuss Hambarine. I wanted to ask you something about that paragraph. You say that on the 22nd of May, 1992, a place called Hambarine was shelled? Would you agree that on the 22nd of May there was still no combat, save for an attack on certain soldiers in a passenger vehicle trying to go through the check-point at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That incident took place between the 22nd and the 23rd, the attack on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you know that some army members were killed at the check-point? Rade Lukic and Radovan Milojica were killed and another four army members were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We could hear it in the media, as well as by way of radio communication in the municipality. We heard about an incident and an exchange of fire, but I was in no position to know of any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Aziz Aliskovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I did not. Perhaps I knew him by face, but not by first and last name. By appearance I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that military organisation was discussed as early as March 1992 in the Prijedor hotel at the level of regional board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was deputy president of the SDA, but I hear of this for the first time from you, and yet I was the deputy president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after -- well, was there a meeting of the regional board of the SDA in the Prijedor hotel in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know. I was not on the regional board. I really don't know. It doesn't sound likely that a meeting with such agenda was held at that time in the Prijedor hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, we can conclude if there was a meeting in March 1992, meeting of the regional SDA board, you were not in attendance and you don't know what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a meeting, I was not in attendance and I don't know what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear about the killing of Radenko Djapa on 1 March 1992 on Kozarska Street in Prijedor. He was a regular policeman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also heard it in the media. I heard about a policeman who was killed and that the non-Serb village of Cerevci was responsibility and that the perpetrator hid there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 3rd of May in Hambarine, a War Staff was formed by the SDA for the area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: A War Staff of the SDA being formed in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the SDA never established any War Staffs. It supported the work and expansion of authority of the legal defence bodies. That was the position of the -- the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what, then, was located in a subterranean bunker located at Borahovo hill?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I hear of that hill for the first time. I've never heard of that name. As for any bunkers, there's no point to discuss anything further then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have no basis, then, to ask you any other questions on that. We'll move onto Kozarac then. The unit commander in Kozarac was Sead Cirkin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Officer Sead Cirkin was in the TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was a professional military person?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only a few months before that period he was included in the war in Croatia where he was wounded and returned home, whereby he joined the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he left the JNA and joined the TO?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a wounded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any shelters built in Kozarac as well as warehouses storing medicine, fuel, food?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I do know, though, that the Serb television broadcast footage of some two or three shelters somewhere in the area of Kozarac. Two or three. Although the area was huge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the attack, before the conflict in Kozarac, did you have any connecting trenches and fortifications built there as well as obstacles placed along roads there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, there was none of that. I heard of certain obstacles placed in parallel with the Serb check-point at Orlovci as well as close to a check-point held by the Serb army in Jakupovici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that a military column was attacked in Jakupovici village?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We heard that on Serb radio. Some denied it, others claimed it was true, but I don't know whether anything happened, and what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the fighting in Kozarac, is it true that Prijedor town itself was attacked on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We heard about a group which arrived from the direction of Hambarine, which had been torched in Prijedor and carried out an infantry attack. We also learned it from the media as well as through different communication channels in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the initial fighting in Kozarac, did you hear that Kemal Alagic led a group which tried to re-take Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I hear about that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that fighting continued in Kozarac throughout May and June?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: May and June?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is not correct, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have wrong information. There was no fighting in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
