utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were sabotage attacks in the area of Kozarac in August and September 1992? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. I know that during August and September, the process of people being taken away and deported from their villages and homes to camps was still under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The policemen who were in Kozarac, did they take part in the fighting on the 24th and the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On the day that this happened, I was at Trnopolje. I didn't go to Kozarac town. I tried to go there but then I went back. Whether there was any such fighting taking place there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have started your answer by saying that you don't know. Then we could have proceeded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 35 you describe the fighting in Kozarac. You were not there, though, and you have no direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please give me some time to look at paragraph 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not describing infantry fighting here that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are talking only about shelling?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the shelling and the burning of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see that on the 25th of May the fighting stopped? Have you noticed that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were several suspensions of fighting that -- some lasted longer, some lasted shorter -- I apologise. I meant shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the inhabitants of Kozarac were called upon to cease fighting during the fighting itself?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Kozarac received announcements and messages and requests via radio, but during the first two or three days there was no Serb army. There couldn't have been any fighting. Only shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You just said you don't know because you were not there. But let me ask you something else: Did you hear any calls upon the civilians of Kozarac to seek shelter in Prijedor until the fighting is over?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the calls for the civilians to be sent to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the fighting many civilians found shelter in Prijedor, both with their relatives and in Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, no pause. Could you please repeat your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sejmenovic, do you know that at that time the wounded from Kozarac arrived at Prijedor hospital, both Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that because I wasn't there physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never heard about that at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard. But that referred to people who were brought from a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please now explain something to us. I'm going to ask you a completely different question. For how long were you in hiding before you went to Trnopolje for the first time? And I don't mean the village. I mean the centre there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, practically from the beginning of the attack on Kozarac until the -- the end of July or the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, where did you stay? Did you stay in one place or in several places? You never explained that. Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I spent most of the time in a house where a Bosniak woman was living, and she was surrounded by houses owned by Ukrainians. For a certain period of time, I spent -- I lived in an unfinished house or in outbuildings or somewhere outdoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You wanted to keep a low profile and not to move too much around. That was the reason why you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 when you describe the refugee columns and what was happening in Trnopolje, and you said that "I saw it all with my own eyes," does it refer only to the initial period when you were headed towards Kozarac and before you went into hiding?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This refers to a period that lasted between 15 and 20 days. But some of the events happened even a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your sources of information were mainly hearsay; that is to say, what you heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about the things that I saw with my own eyes. And my encounter with the refugee columns and the so-called ethnic cleansing. I saw that on several occasions. Allow me, please, to make it easier for you. Sometimes I didn't have time to run away, and I had to hide very close to a road or in a building close to a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, when you said that you were hiding in two houses, in fact, or outdoors in the vicinity of those houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was within the radius of between 250 and 300 metres. But this is a point where three or four villages converge. That is a junction between these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, back to 36. You say: "The Serb infantry advanced, driving people out, and killing stragglers letters in villages." Now this killing people in villages, which villages did you have in mind? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group of refugees in the village of Sivci, and when the army entered the village to drive them out, they killed a few people. I was about a kilometre away and some people came to the house of Dzemal Sivac, where I was, and they gave us this information. Later on while I was walking during the night I came across those graves. On another occasion, I was watching the cleansing of the village of Mujkanovici. I was in close proximity and I saw everything. However, no one was killed on that occasion. What happened was that after the shooting people were lined up into a column and were driven to Kozarac, and this was accompanied by singing of songs and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the Serb army, Serb police, or Serb TO in the area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean deployed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I mean on the move. Because you were moving around the area and watching all this.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On three separate occasions I saw these developments because I was on the run, and I said I didn't have enough time to run away. I tried to hide as much as possible and watch this. On one occasion I went into an old shed and I heard army personnel talking, and they wanted to open a garage and take a car that was inside it by shooting at the door, and during that I had an occasion to hear them talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 37 now. You say: "Some soldiers wore Martic militia uniforms, others JNA uniforms, others uniforms of the 5th Kozara Brigade. Others wore civilian clothes." Those wearing civilian clothes, were they armed as well?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The top was, for the main part, a military outfit. These people were carrying weapons and they were joining them in actions with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between the uniform of the soldiers of the 5th Kozara Brigade and the JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: JNA soldiers were more neat and cleaner. They were similar, the uniforms I mean. But they also behaved themselves in a different way. They were more disciplined and their demeanour was better. The other soldiers were less disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about the difference --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the 5 Kozara Brigade had old reservist --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only difference was in the uniforms between those who were on APCs and those who were in infantry. As for Martic's people, Martic's men, they were dressed in some slightly different uniforms, with lighter pattern. I know that because even before the war, I saw some people from Prijedor who were dressed in Martic's uniforms, and I saw them in a restaurant when they were drinking, so that led me to believe that these uniforms were present there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 38, you say: The women and children were in Trnopolje or in some places where groups of refugees had gathered. A few days later, an army arrived and killed a number of people. Were you yourself present at these locations when the army came and killed a few people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. At two locations where the refugees were, and at one location where one woman was killed and another was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where was all that taking place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Some old men and old women were killed in Circi [phoen] village. There was a huge group of refugees. One old man was killed in front of the entire group, and then close to the house another two or three people were killed. I heard shots. I heard this was happening but I wasn't present. It was only later that I stumbled upon those graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was in mid- -- or, rather, beginning of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: July, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it might have been early July 1992. Another location where people were killed or, rather, a woman was killed, was some 500 metres from the place where I was hiding. While they were driving people out of the village, they killed a woman in her garden. She -- she was not a Muslim, but due to the fact that the villages that they were vacating were close by, I think that that's the reason why they shot her because they believed her to be a Muslim as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to repeat what he said about the first occasion. You said: "Some old men and old women were killed in ..." And then you mentioned the village where there was a huge group of refugees. Could you please repeat what village you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sivci village. And there was quite a large group of refugee there. It's S-I-V-C-I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I think you earlier referred to Sivci village, but have I difficulties in finding it. You've told us about graves you've seen in Sivci. Is that the same you are talking about or is it a different event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- it's the same place. But was it also the same event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The same event and I'm talking about a few graves that were hastily dug out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the village is spelled as C-I-V-I-C-E rather than Sivci. But you are talking about the same event? Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, these graves where, according to you, people were buried immediately after the killing --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: These people were buried by other refugees. The army had already passed. That was in late afternoon or early evening. The army passed through looking for men and looking for particular individuals. They killed a few people. And then the refugees buried these people in a rush next to a religious facility. These men and women were buried there. During the following day, Sivci were completely empty. There were no refugees anymore. I don't know exactly the location where these graves were, and during the night I just stumbled upon this mound of earth, or, rather, these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not speak to those people at all about the murders.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean those people who came to Dzemal Sivac's house and who spoke to me and the woman in whose house I stayed? They -- they said what had been going on over there. They also told me some details, if you want ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say they evacuated this refugee column and these people came to the same woman's house. What does it mean, "evacuate the refugee column"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They came at one or two days later so that after that there was nobody left in Sivci, and the woman in whose house I was hiding had to leave because she was threatened by the army, and after that I remained completely alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which unit were these armed men from; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the armed men who entered Sivci village?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 39. You say: "Serb forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina and others did the same job, the same procedure, the same consequences." And then you paint a general picture. You did not see these events for yourself? These are your conclusions, inferences?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Some events I did observe from a smaller or greater distance. And I know about a few others from other people. And what I saw in those three cases, the procedure was the same. The way events unfolded was the same. And I could see what happened in the Novikamovici [phoen] village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you make your inferences based on what you know and you told us today that you don't know many of these things, such as military organising, arming, et cetera. You do not know if there had been fighting in specific villages where you say people were expelled or evacuated. You don't know how or if they were armed. You don't know which fighting went on, who participated in it, which military forces, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the place I was and the area where I was, I have already said what I know. And I do know the answers to most of your questions. However, concerning villages that were 15, 20 kilometres away, especially in that period of isolation, I could not possibly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move to letter J above paragraph 143 where you speak about Trnopolje. You entered Trnopolje camp unnoticed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you crawled below some sort of wire. Is that how you entered?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I crawled through a ditch or a canal, and it took just one step to crawl under the wire. It was some sort of berry wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the area where people were placed was not fenced in on all sides?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some parts were just surrounded by a very low fence, several dozen centimetres?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of it was in a clearing, but it was covered by a machine-gun nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 44: "Trnopolje camp was supervised by a military organisation."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware - at least that's what the documentation says - that the police took over the security over the centre from the army? Or were they just uniformed men to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The man to whom I surrendered was an army officer, Lieutenant Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, Kuruzovic was the camp commander, whereas the officer to whom I surrendered and who took me to the command and later to the military police nearby Keraterm was a lieutenant by rank. His first name was Slavko. In addition to Slavko, there were other soldiers there, so he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. To which unit did he belong?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I could not possibly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you entered at that time, was that place totally disorganised?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At that point, yes. But before that, there was strict discipline; the lining up of men, and roll-calls by first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now paragraph 45, please. You describe the reasons why other people came to Trnopolje. Did people come to Trnopolje of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Some groups did come on their own, after the torching of neighbouring houses and the torchings and killings in other villages. After that, they had information that the only safe place, the only safe thing to do was to go to Trnopolje, and some people indeed did come there that way. But that was a smaller part, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 46, if you can have a look at it, you talk about the killing of an old man, a young woman, and rapes. You did not see any of these things. You were not there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was there when six people were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is paragraph 47. I'm talking about 46. Have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know I had a brief contact with the lady doctor who was there, a veterinarian in fact. I know that they were present and that they offered assistance. Of the killings, I heard the ones I name in paragraph 46. I was not there because they happened before I came to Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move to paragraph 47 where you describe these six people bearing the last name of Foric. How many men took them away?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Let me see. As far as I was able to see, because it was already dark, I think three men took them away. Whether somebody else was waiting behind the tractor, I don't know. I only know that one of them was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you say today three men. In your statement, you say two. One soldier, one policeman.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat. This is how it was. It was dark. One soldier had come before to see the Forics, talk to them, and went away. Now it is dark. A policeman comes and a soldier comes. They're standing on the edge behind the tractor. It's my impression that there are more people there. They order one Foric to call the other brothers and have them put their footwear on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've told us this already. Just how many men took the Forics away?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Two, possibly more. It was dark and I was not quite free to lift my head and look around to see if there were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because in the Tadic case, transcript of the 24th of May 1996, page 1390, or perhaps it's the next page, 1391, you said that four people took the Forics away.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then it must be four. Because my memory was much fresher then. And two -- two of them did the talking with the Forics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I should like to move to the documents you discussed with the Prosecution. We don't need to call up in e-court. It's P290. That's a decision of the Executive Council of Prijedor municipality to dismiss Mirza Muftic from work. It is signed by Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see in e-court, please, for example, 65 ter, 07105. And then I will put my question. This document is also a document of the Executive Board, also signed by Dr. Milan Kovacevic as president of the Executive Board, and it is about the dismissal of Milenko Djukanovic, economist, from his post of director of the socially owned company Zagreb Voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Milenko Djukanovic was a Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. That's what his name indicates, but I suppose it's from some other party, not the SDS, and that's the reason for his dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you brought this document up at paragraph 59, line 22 to line 25, or to line 62, you say: "Very well. Now I should like to move to the documents you discussed. We don't need to call up in e-court. It's P290."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "It is the decision of the Prijedor [microphone not activated] it is signed by Dr. Kovacevic. Can we see in e-court, please, for example, 65 ter 07105." Now when you say "for example," I'm not quite sure what -- are we seeing here P292 or are we seeing 07105.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we see 07105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because it's from the same set and we made it -- we stipulated yesterday that there is more documents like we saw yesterday, like P290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have no objection if the document is being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I still had to decide -- we had to decide on admission. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07105 becomes Exhibit D62, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D62 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecution showed you a document, P289, and we would need to see it again in e-court. You discussed this document with the Prosecution. It's dated 1st July 1992. The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina passed this decision saying, in item 1 - and that's what you said - that senior positions, leading positions, can be held only by Serb cadres. In item 2 we read also these posts may not be held by Serbs either who did not confirm in the referendum -- who did not confirm it in the referendum and are not idealogically clear that the only representative of the Serbian people is the SDS. Do you notice this?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this was taken two months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it grounds -- I don't mean legal grounds, but is it also a basis for non-acceptance that somebody does not belong to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's the way you can understand it. That's what this document of the Crisis Staff says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we saw P291, and we can look at it again. This is a photograph of a thin man, and you said that was approximately what people in Trnopolje looked like.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I said the majority of them. Most of them, depending on how long they had been in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see in e-court 1D350.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see a whole group of people here.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The one on the right is even on the chubby side. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: None of the people in this picture look like the man you had discussed earlier from the previous photograph shown you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on when he was deported. Some had been there a month and a half, two months, whereas others were deported later from other parts of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record we see the ERN number here on this photograph, the still we took from the video. It's V000-0664. And we could perhaps see if we could see the bottom of the still from which time sequence the still was made. We would also like to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D00350 becomes Exhibit D63, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I think the parties - and I'm also addressing the Prosecution - certainly also addressing the Prosecution, better refrain from showing one man who is badly fed and then the other party shows someone who could needs some --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Workout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some workout. I mean, that's, from an evidentiary ponit of view is, of course, is -- and again, I was about to say it yesterday, that doesn't help. It doesn't assist. Because what we are talking about is about the main impression these persons made and giving examples and then to ask, Is this how it looked? I mean, the Chamber has an imagination of how it looks if you are underfed. But since the Prosecution tendered it, since the Defence now tenders another picture, it is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have more but we will refrain from showing them and introducing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- no, you could compete. Ten pictures of thin people, ten pictures of well-fed people. I hope that you understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that we were not -- Mr. Traldi, I hope you understand as well. Please proceed. I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a good time to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be a good time for a break, and we first would like the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the witness is escorted, I can tell Mr. Traldi that he'll have some time for his additional -- or re-direct, if he needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Sejmenovic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, we are near the end. I have another document. Yesterday you commented upon Exhibit P288.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it brought up. It is dated the 30th of April, 1992, issued by the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It refers to the takeover and how many police stations had been mobilised. Do you recall that, at that time, the MUP had already been split in two?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, split in two?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had certain MUP members left or were they divided? On that date, were you still working together?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was on the day of the takeover. On that day, they no longer worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You spent several days in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was any food provided in Trnopolje? Food that was not procured by the people there themselves? Was there a mess or a kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that they brought some bread which was insufficient, and then it was approved for the people to go to the nearby houses and bring in foodstuff to prepare food for themselves. Some people also received permission to go and catch cattle, which was roaming free by that time in order to have the meat prepared in cauldrons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice people who had lice? Did they have dysentery, typhus?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In Omarska there were a great many people with dysentery. In Trnopolje itself, well, I had no opportunity to see because I was in one place only while I was there covered for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you see anything?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know there were many sick people but I can't tell what you they were sick of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me. I'm trying to wrap things up. [In English] Sorry for this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stay with the topic of relationship vis-a-vis the JNA. The deadline for JNA units to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina was the 19th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was around mid-May or in the second half of May, but I don't recall a specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that most officers following JNA departure from Bosnia-Herzegovina remained, those who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do know that some Muslim officers were from Serbia and Sandzak, such as Sefer Halilovic and Ramiz Drekovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who made the decision on organising, training, and arming of units known as the Green Berets or the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Patriotic League? What do you know on that score?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know quite a lot as regards Prijedor. As for the state as a whole, I know that the TO was an armed formation which received instruction from the level of the top of the state. They had their command and structure in Sarajevo and they were a legitimate force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were established?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know there were some groups in other parts of the country later on which organised themselves by way of self-defence. But I can't discuss any details. There are people who are far more competent to speak on that topic. In Prijedor, such organisations did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were many attacks on the JNA before its departure from Bosnia-Herzegovina? There were attacks in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the things that were common knowledge is what I knew as well. I know about conflict in Tuzla, and I know something about Sarajevo later on when the war broke out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who made such decisions, to have the JNA attacked? Could you get any such information at SDA meetings?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, attacks on the JNA? It's a one-sided interpretation because the other side had a different one and there are still disputes to this day. I'd rather not go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope it is -- not in dispute that if an officer's wife is attacked -- well, did you hear about that? I hope there's no dispute as to who attacked whom, if a child or the wife of an officer was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on an interpretation of the sides that are involved. I would really like to stay out of that domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time of attack in Prijedor on 30th of May, 1992, most of the 43rd Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade was at the front line in Croatia or deployed along the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know that some of those soldiers were in Posavina. They had been there before. As for the front in Croatia, at least as far as the 5th Kozara Brigade area, the fighting had already ceased there because the army had control over that territory. There was no serious fighting there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something on a tangential matter. At paragraph 58 - it is P283 - you say that you were interviewed by two Serbian journalists.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you say that one of them promised you a written text of the interview so that you would be able to read it. You say that you read out that text in front of a camera. Where in the interview can we see that you are -- were reading a text?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that footage. I can't -- you can't see it. It was Zoran Mutic from Prijedor. He came one day, had a conversation with me. He told me of his intention and told me that he would prepare a text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now repeating what you said in your statement. Mr. Lukic, where in the interview can we see? You mean the video of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we received, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the interview. Yes. Well, what you'd -- what you expect the witness to -- is it visible, is it not visible? Have you reviewed the video of that interview, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not, Your Honour. I'd like to, though, but I had no opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it may be difficult for the witness to answer your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have reviewed it and that is why I'm asking you, since I did not come across that part. And today you told us that it was not among your interviews. After that, Mr. Kupresanin arrived and took you away. You were taken from Omarska to where?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: To the municipal building and his office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And later you were at some address?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosanska Vrbanja where my sister and brother-in-law lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for our understanding, is that interview in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have several interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but I'm not sure now [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apparently --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in the evidence. I've never seen this gentleman reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in any interview I saw with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But of course the Chamber will have to evaluate the evidence. You are suggesting that he is not reliable when he says that he was reading. That's the clear suggestion in your question. Now a witness cannot -- it's unfair to a witness unless you show him that interview, and if -- and show it to the Chamber as well so that we can assess what we see and whether that affects in any way the reliability. But you can't just put that to the witness to suggest that he's not telling us the truth and then leave it to that. And of course if the witness leaves, then, of course, he is unable to further comment on it, and that is -- again is -- at a later stage, you could not rely on saying, Look at the video, we don't see anything, because the witness could have told us otherwise perhaps. We do not know. But this is not the way to proceed. That's what I would like to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not prepare. Otherwise I would have to prepare all the videos we have with this witness. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I wouldn't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say I reviewed it, I don't see him reading anywhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- then at least you could have a list of the videos and then ask Mr. Traldi whether he at any point in time sees the witness reading and then agree on it or give it to the Chamber so that we could have a look at it. But how to resolve it is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- our primary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not the main point of my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went to your sister's and brother-in-law's where you stayed until the end of that year; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 14th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there, you went --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Banja Luka with the assistance of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your sister and brother-in-law remained there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: For a while. Until they got an opportunity to get out and they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. While you were staying with them, were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was suggested to me that I better stay indoors without venturing outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Traldi, let me first confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I'd like to start with one of the last topics in cross-examination, and we'll play a clip from 65 ter 22615 which has been labelled 65 ter 22615B. We'll that the entire clip first in accordance with the recent guide-lines on videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at least you want to rely on text spoken. If it is about looking whether someone seems to be reading, then I might not even need any text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will ask a couple of questions about the text as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before it will be played for the second time, could I ask the witness: Is this one of the two interviews with journalist Mutic, or is it the interview by Dragan Bozanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Dragan Bozanic's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, I take it that you want to have it played for a second time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we'll start that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The British journalist did not want to film the infirmary of this centre, nor were they interested in prisoner Mevludin Sejmenovic, a former deputy of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly and an activist of the SDA. "We have heard that you are one of the rare members or -- or rather occupants of this reception centre who came here to Omarska of his own accord? "Sejmenovic: Yes, precisely. "Reporter: Could you explain for what reasons, why you came? "Sejmenovic: Well, I came after waiting for a while in hiding so that the main perpetrators of all those horrible event could be caught; so that the whole truth about the entire incident could be established; so that the truth could be established about the people who committed all this evil; so that my work and the statements that I will give will be believed. "Reporter: Who are you referring to when you say they should be caught? Who is to blame for all this, all this horror that happened here the region? "Sejmenovic: I mean primarily the leader of the Party of the Bosnian Krajina, the president of the region, Mirza Mujadzic, and the president of the party in Prijedor, also Mirza Mujadzic, and the member of the executive committee for Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the people in the party who organised all these war tasks, war affairs. "Reporter: Do your colleagues, those who are here with you in the centre, know -- do they know your opinion? Can you say what you think openly about all this -- why all this evil has befallen the Muslim people? "Sejmenovic: I have already spoken about it twice here in conversations with people and in an interview for the Krajina television. I've already given my statements and I have given -- sent a message to the people with respect to this entire situation that I am observing directly on the spot in Bosnian Krajina, that means in Prijedor. I'm not observing it with a telescope as do those who are the main architects of this evil. "Reporter: I don't know if you have had an opportunity to see the foreign journalists, mostly from Great Britain, who are visiting this centre here, and the reason is that there have been reports in the world in the past few days that there are in the Serbian republic, that is the area where you are now, that there are concentration camps for Muslims and Croats. Since you are here in the centre and you say you came here of your own accord, would you tell these foreign journalists what the truth is, and do you know whether it is indeed a concentration camp? Is this a concentration camp or is this a collection centre? What could you tell them? "Sejmenovic: Well, I could tell them that the war operations resulted in such consequences that made it necessary to group people both for security reasons and for mere survival. Ultimately speaking. And that this does not have the features of a concentration camp as it is described by political propaganda, and I think they could see all that with their own eyes today. "Reporter: One more question. Before the -- before the war, flared up for real here, did anyone among the Muslim people in this area prepare for war? "Sejmenovic: There was -- there had been talk over the months before in everyday conversations among ordinary people who have nothing to do with politics and certainly in the political parties, including the SDA, about weapons because there was a great amount of fear and uncertainty and people were looking for some kind of support then. In conversations people talked about their personal safety and so on. But it's abundantly clear that political oligarchies did a lot of shady business behind the backs of their own membership and the entire people. Their aim was probably to push people into some kind of struggle for their own personal or individual interests, not reckoning with the real consequences that could result from all that or even counting on them and working precisely for that purpose. I don't know. "Reporter: Since the foreigners are already concluding that this war in our territories has all the features of a religious war, have you heard that certain Muslim priests - and Hodzas and Imams - had special US made weapons for killing game already before the war? "Sejmenovic: I really don't know about arming or weapons, and we have already discussed that for a long time. There's every evidence of that. But from talk among ordinary people and today after everything, there is evidence that a number of priests were involved in the arming or smuggling of weapons or in some other way. I don't know. But I know that by doing so they have probably violated the norms and regulations of the religion they preach and the norms of human ethnics and that they deserve, quote/unquote, some credit for all this evil that has happened to all the peoples. Not just one."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, it was probably implicit in your response to the President's question, but just for the record, did you recognise the man in the T-shirt speaking during this video?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you recognise the journalist who was interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's Dragan Bozanic, a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you were given a text to read into the camera, which journalist was interviewing you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, this is clear from the transcript, isn't it? From the -- from the statement. Mr. Mutic gave him a text to be read and he was also interviewed by someone else. And the same, of course, to ask who was the person in the T-shirt. Of course he is announced as such, we can see it, of course, unless there would be any very special thing to believe that it was someone else if he is called by the name of this witness. Let's try to go -- come to the substance as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I'll move to the things you say during the video, then, sir. And the things you say in the video are surprising, and I want to ask you about a couple of them. First, you agree with the reporter that you came to Omarska voluntarily. Was that an accurate statement of how you felt at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you seemed to say that Omarska was necessary and that people were grouped there for safety. Is that a true statement of what you believed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is an untruthful representation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how did you feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think after that fact is clarified that it's not Mutic, this does not come from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd say the video is within the scope of cross-examination. He cross-examined on the relevant paragraphs as well as the video interview, but I'm in your hands in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're right. If the Prosecution would have wanted to show us this video in addition to the statement, they have had an opportunity to do so. And, Mr. Traldi, the cross-examination was about the reading of the statement and that was a different interview, and you now show us the other interview. That was exactly the reason why I asked immediately after the first playing which of the interviews this was. Please proceed. Do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Just about five brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- again all the parties are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will be as efficient as I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Beginning on temporary transcript page 26, Mr. Sejmenovic, Mr. Lukic questioned you about the participation of military officers in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the Court Officer to call back up document 1D00323, which is also 65 ter 07104. I'd ask that we turn to Article 9 on page 4 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That article reads: "The Crisis Staff shall maintain constant co-operation with units of the JNA, the Territorial Defence, Civilian Protection, and the Public Security System via the senior officers of these institutions and organs." And sir, my question for you is: Is this consistent with your observations of the relationship between the Crisis Staff and Serb forces in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object again, Your Honour. My question was whether these gentlemen were members of Crisis Staff, not whether they co-operated or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's so clearly related to the matter that your objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence is willing to stipulate to it then I will happily withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's an invitation, Mr. Lukic whether you would stipulate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not the witness, I think, who was invited. Stipulation that this is what is found in Article 9 on page 4. Is that what you want the Defence to stipulate on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To the co-operation between the military and the Crisis Staff in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that it is in the document or whether they co-operated? I mean, the relationship is described by the witness in the statement. We're now talking about what is found in the document. If -- but let's -- the document is tendered and is in evidence, isn't it, Mr. Lukic? Yes. Now whether in paragraph 9 these words are found, why do we need a stipulation? This Chamber, I will put on my glasses, we can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I'll withdraw the invitation and just ask that the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question is whether that's found in paragraph 9? I still don't have it on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The question is whether that was consistent with his observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At pages 36 and 37 of today's transcript, Mr. Lukic suggested to you that only policemen worked in Omarska. In paragraph 55 of your statement, Exhibit P283, you say there were soldiers marching up and down the areas where the prisoners were. Where did you see these soldiers specifically?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the soldiers on the tarmac. Some of them were entering the hangar, some were coming out. When I was taken to the white house soldiers came to beat me. Soldiers also entered the room next to the green house [as interpreted]. And they were positioned along the route between Omarska and the camp itself, and it was equipped with sandbags and machine-gun nests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At transcript page 49, Mr. Lukic asked if you heard that Muslim wounded from Kozarac were brought to the Prijedor hospital. You said: "Yes, I heard, but that referred to people from a different area." My question is: Does that mean that you did not hear that wounded Muslims from Kozarac were brought to the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I literally said this. I don't know about Kozarac but I heard that certain individuals were taken from -- to the hospital, individuals from other regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And finally, sir, Mr. Lukic and His Honour inquired about arming the Kozarac TO, and you replied by mentioning in part the ultimatum you received from Major Zeljaja. My question for you in this regard is: During the meeting you had with Colonel Arsic, Major Zeljaja, Mr. Miskovic, and others at the Prijedor SDS headquarters - or at any point after that - did any of the Serb authorities give the impression that if you surrendered whatever weapons you had, regardless of the number, an attack on Kozarac could be avoided?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they did not display any indication or any gesture of goodwill that would give us some hope, and they instead issued an ultimatum which was impossible to fulfil and any attempt on our part would end up in failure to fulfil this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to put something right on the record. The -- Mr. Traldi, you called back the document 1D00323, that was the one with paragraph 9 in it, but that was not tendered by Mr. Lukic. He read a portion of it. It is the same, as you say, 65 ter 07104. Would the parties like to have that in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, so that the Bench can read it as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you were the first one to refer to it. Shall we make a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll let Mr. Traldi have it as their exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, how generous you are today, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I decided that it will be Defence exhibit. It would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D323 becomes Exhibit D64, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D64 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one question for this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the booth because you're all adding to my bad reputation, and the interviewer in the video said one more question and then he put another five. If you limit it to one question, Mr. Lukic, please do ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I still have to trouble you for a while longer. Those soldiers in Omarska, you've already told us you don't know which unit they were from, but did you conclude about their affiliation to the army only on the basis of uniform too?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Also from the way they expressed themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody comes in and says, You will now see how the army beats, and there's a policeman next to him in a blue uniform, I can only conclude that he is from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Sejmenovic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague - it wasn't the first time - and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and hopefully you'll safely return home. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, if you allow me, Your Honour. I want to express my great gratitude to you after giving testimony in this courtroom many times. I want to express my thankfulness to you for the great work you are doing on my -- in my own name and on behalf of all these people who expect justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We appreciate that are you following and that you are positive on the work of this Tribunal. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I again would like to apologise to interpreters and those others assisting us. You well understand that we tried to conclude the testimony of this witness today, but it -- with a little bit of assistance of the parties, we would have been less beyond quarter past 2.00. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 4th of October, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of October, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.24 p.m.,
